title: cpu-side-bottlenecks-python-profiling-notes
summary: Notes and experimental results from CPU-side profiling focused on tokenization, request parsing, thread-pool contention, and Python overhead for the serving runtime. Includes reproducible microbenchmarks, tools used, flamegraph snippets, and recommended mitigations.
background: We observed elevated CPU utilization on CPU-bound stages of the request path even when GPU token generation is active. Tail latency spikes correlate with large batches + many small, concurrent requests. Goal: identify hotspots on the CPU side that increase overall request latency and reduce throughput, and validate mitigations that reduce per-request CPU cost.
methodology_and_tools: Overview: run controlled load tests against the serving runtime in a staging cluster, then profile representative services. Tools: Linux perf, perf script + FlameGraph, py-spy (sampling), cProfile (instrumentation), tracemalloc (allocations), strace (syscall noise), BPF tools (bcc), and a small set of microbenchmarks in pytest/bench. We run: 1) full-stack end-to-end requests through the REST handler (JSON parse, routing, tokenizer, model request enqueue, etc.), 2) isolated tokenization microbenchmarks (HuggingFace tokenizers & rust tokenizers), 3) request-parsing microbenchmarks (fastjson vs python json), 4) thread-pool concurrency stress tests (varying worker counts), 5) Python GIL/multiprocessing experiments.
key_findings: 1) Tokenization is a non-trivial fraction of CPU for short prompts: ~25-40% of CPU time per request for inputs < 32 tokens when using the Python tokenizer wrapper. 2) JSON request parsing (request body -> python dict) accounted for ~10-18% of CPU and increased p95 by ~12ms under high concurrency. Using a faster C-backed parser reduced that by ~8-10ms. 3) Thread pool contention observed in the request path: the default concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor had noticeable queuing at >200 concurrent requests; switching to a tuned worker pool improved latency and throughput. 4) Python overhead (object churn, allocation, GC pauses) surfaces in flamegraphs around the handler boundary — many small allocations when building response metadata and token buffers. 5) GIL limits multi-threaded CPU parallelism: pure-Python CPU work does not scale linearly with threads; using multiprocessing showed better CPU utilization but increased memory and latency variance. 6) Switching tokenization to Rust bindings (rust-tokenizers via FFI) reduced tokenization CPU by ~3x in microbenchmarks.
benchmarks_details:
Representative numbers from staging (m5.4xlarge-like CPU profile, 8 vCPU, 32GB):
- Baseline (py tokenizer, python json, ThreadPoolExecutor default): p50 latency = 42ms, p95 = 118ms, CPU secs/request = 0.014.
- Tokenizer-only microbench (input 16 tokens, 10k runs): py-tokenizer = 95us/op, rust-tokenizer = 28us/op, speedup ~3.4x.
- JSON parse comparison (payload ~1.5KB): python json.loads = 210us/op, orjson = 70us/op.
- Thread pool stress (100, 200, 400 concurrent requests): queuing start point for default pool ~200 concurrent. With tuned pool (max_workers = min(32, os.cpu_count() * 5), prioritized FIFO) queuing reduced and p95 improved ~18%.
- Multiprocessing test (4 worker processes) vs multithread: multiprocessing improved throughput by ~1.9x for CPU-bound tokenization + parsing workloads but increased 99th percentile latency variability by ~22% due to inter-process scheduling and copy-on-write at start-up.
- Memory/allocations: average allocations per request (baseline) ~420 small objects; after micro-optimizations (reuse buffers, avoid intermediate dicts) allocations dropped to ~130 and GC pauses reduced by ~5-8ms at p99.
profiling_notes:
Flamegraph hotspots (sampling):
- ~30% spent in 'py_tokenizer/_tokenize' C-extension wrapper and Python glue.
- ~12% in json.loads (pure-python path) and application-level validation.
- ~10% in 'concurrent.futures.threading' when threads are idle/waiting on locks under contention.
- ~8% in response-building code (looping through tokens, creating small dicts).
Py-spy snapshots confirm heavy allocation in helper functions that format per-token metadata. Perf shows syscalls (epoll/poll) negligible except under extreme concurrency where epoll wakeups cause small spikes. Tracemalloc reveals most allocations come from list/dict growth during response construction.
root_causes: 1) Tokenizer integration: using the Python wrapper around a C tokenizer adds allocation and copying overhead; not using the fastest available tokenizer (rust or batch-mode) wastes CPU. 2) Request parsing/validation done synchronously in Python on the request thread instead of delegating to C-parsers or parsing lazily. 3) ThreadPool defaults were not tuned for our workload shape (many short CPU-bound tasks + IO), causing lock contention and queueing overhead. 4) Python object churn in response formatting causes GC pressure and tail latency spikes. 5) GIL prevents horizontal CPU scaling inside a single process for CPU-bound stages.
mitigations_and_experiments:
We ran targeted changes and measured impact: 
- Replace python tokenizer wrapper with rust-tokenizers FFI (via pyo3): tokenization CPU dropped ~3x, p95 improved ~9-14ms for short prompts. Tradeoffs: increased binary size and extra build complexity.
- Swap json.loads for orjson in the request parser: JSON parse time down from ~210us to ~70us; p95 improved ~8-10ms in E2E tests. orjson also reduced allocations.
- Move request validation (schema checks) to a compiled validator (fastjsonschema) and perform only minimal checks synchronously; expensive checks deferred to background checks for non-critical fields.
- Rework thread pool: experiment with two-layer executor: small dedicated pool for sync CPU-bound pre-processing (tokenization/parsing) implemented as multiprocessing Pool with worker process pinning, and an async loop for IO/model RPCs (uvloop). Observed ~1.7x throughput improvement for mixed workloads.
- Reduce object churn: reuse bytearray buffers for tokenizer output, build responses using array.array/memoryview where possible, and avoid per-request list concatenations. Allocations down ~70%.
- Introduce prefix-token cache for common prompts: cache pre-tokenized prefix for templates; hit-rate ~18% on internal traffic, reduced CPU per request by ~12%.
- Consider moving critical pre-processing into a small Rust service behind a local Unix socket (lower latency than RPC) to avoid Python overhead entirely for tokenization and heavy validations.
tradeoffs:
- Multiprocessing reduces GIL contention but increases memory footprint and process startup costs.
- FFI to Rust reduces CPU but increases build complexity and potential deployment friction for private customers.
- Moving logic out of the main process adds more moving parts to deploy and monitor.
- Caching reduces CPU but increases memory and cache invalidation complexity.
recommendations:
Short-term (low friction):
- Replace json.loads with orjson across request path.
- Introduce orjson + fastjsonschema for validation to cut parse/validation CPU.
- Tune ThreadPoolExecutor defaults (increase max_workers, use LIFO for short tasks) and measure under load.
- Add tokenization cache for common prefixes and templates (TTL-based).

Medium-term: 
- Integrate rust-tokenizers via pyo3 for the hot path (tokenization). Target: reduce tokenization CPU by ~3x for short prompts.
- Rework pre-processing pipeline: perform heavy sync CPU work in pinned worker processes (multiprocessing) and keep the main process event-loop focused on async IO.

Long-term: 
- Offer an optional small native preprocessor service (Rust) shipped with Dedicated/Private deployments to remove Python-bound bottlenecks.
- Add e2e benchmarks to CI that measure CPU secs/request for short prompts and raise alerts if regressions >10%.

full_text:
CPU-side bottlenecks - profiling notes

Objective:
Surface and quantify CPU-side bottlenecks in the serving runtime for short/medium prompts where GPU time is not dominant. We focused on tokenization, request parsing, thread pool behavior, and Python overhead.

Context:
Our customers rely on low tail latency. We saw cases where GPU was underutilized but p95 was elevated due to CPU pre/post processing. Fixing CPU overhead directly improves p50/p95 and reduces unit cost.

Experimental setup:
- Staging cluster that mirrors Dedicated compute (8 vCPU, 32GB).
- Load generator: wrk2 + custom client to vary concurrency and input sizes.
- Profiling capture: perf + py-spy during steady-state runs.
- Microbench harness in repo under tests/bench/tokenization_bench.py.

Detailed notes and logs (condensed):
- Tokenizer: the Python wrapper copies bytes into Python objects; using the rust tokenizer via pyo3 both avoids copies and exposes a batch API. Measured 95us/op -> 28us/op on 16-token inputs. For short prompts this is the single biggest win.
- Request parsing: many endpoints accept JSON payloads; switching to orjson and deferring non-critical validation reduces synchronous CPU.
- Thread pools: default ThreadPoolExecutor has contention at scale; our workload is many tiny CPU tasks followed by network to GPU. Using a smaller, faster pool for pre-processing and leaving async event loop for IO produced best results.
- Python overhead: response assembly created many small lists/dicts per token. Reusing buffers and building simple bytearrays cut allocations.

Appendix: quick repro commands
- Tokenizer microbenchmark: python -m tests.bench.tokenizer --impl=py --size=16 --runs=10000
- JSON parse microbenchmark: python -m tests.bench.json_parse --impl=python|orjson --payload=1536
- Capture flamegraph: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 30; sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg

Notes for reviewers:
- Numbers are from staging and will vary by instance type. Focus more on relative wins (3x tokenizer speed, 2x for orjson) than absolute latency.
- Priority: orjson (low risk), executor tuning (low-medium risk), tokenization FFI (medium risk, bigger wins).

If you want a short checklist to ship: 
- Hotfix: orjson switch + observability metric (CPU secs/request)
- Spike: rust-tokenizer + packaging validation
- Canary: hybrid worker pool (multiprocess pinned)

End of notes.
